articles.title: As Paramount Settlement Talks With States Progress, Some AGs Are Pushing for Stronger Restrictions
articles.summary: On Sunday, settlement talks between Paramount and the state attorneys general that sued to block its Warner Bros. Discovery deal continued — but there was no resolution by the end of the day.
body: The terms discussed were said to include Paramount agreeing to operate Warner Bros.’ studio operations separately for a time (something Paramount chief David Ellison already said he was willing to do). Also on the table was a requirement that the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. release at least 30 films theatrically per year (a promise Ellison has already made, repeatedly), with financial penalties if they fail to hit that mark. In addition, the two sides also discussed a binding guarantee from Paramount that it would not relocate its existing California operations (as Ellison has threatened to do) and the formation of a third-party “editorial adviser” to oversee CNN and CBS News.

New York Attorney General Letitia James, for one, wants Paramount to commit to specific job-protection guarantees, including for employees at Warner Bros., sources confirmed. Paramount has claimed it would achieve $6 billion in cost savings by merging with WBD — and that would imply thousands of layoffs.

articles.title: ’60 Minutes’ Patrick Clancy Interview Provides a Surprisingly Thoughtful Take on Much-Watched Trial
articles.summary: Credit is merited when it’s due: CBS News’ newly minted “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat landed a thoughtful, emotional interview with the person who may have elicited more speculation than anyone else this year.
body: What’s been most interesting, to this viewer of the trial from afar, about the story is Patrick’s ability to forgive his ex-wife for what she has admitted to doing to their family. Douthat asked about that: Patrick has forgiven Lindsay, even though she did not ask for it. Were Douthat, perhaps, a more seasoned question-asker on camera, he might have asked how often the two speak and what else passes between them. Douthat let opportunities like this go.

With that in mind, Douthat deserves praise for being genuinely thoughtful and curious about how Patrick Clancy is doing these days. This was the interview every TV outlet sought, and “60 Minutes” can be doubly proud: Its name and heritage may well have helped book the most-talked-about figure of the moment, and its on-camera talent was more open to deep questions than to relitigating the legal case. The question remaining is whether, in weeks between massive gets that exist entirely outside the narrative of an increasingly unpopular presidency whose functionaries Weiss courts, “60 Minutes” can maintain this momentum.

articles.title: Ke Huy Quan Says His $100,000 ‘Indiana Jones’ Residual Check Was ‘Life-Changing’ As a Child Actor: It ‘Didn’t Make Any Sense’
articles.summary: Ke Huy Quan shared in his new memoir, “Never Say Die,” the feeling of receiving his first residual check of $100,000 for “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” as a child actor. Because Quan was just 12 years old when he booked the role of Short Round in the 1984 film (his first major
body: “One afternoon, I walked into the kitchen and found my parents standing together at the table,” Quan wrote in the memoir via Entertainment Weekly. “Mom was holding an envelope with my name printed across it. Dad had the papers that had been inside.”

“Back then, almost no actors got a piece of a movie’s profits,” Quan continued. “Even today, only the biggest stars do. That a kid like me, making his first film, would be included in something like that was unheard of. And ‘Temple of Doom’ wasn’t some small movie no one was expected to see. It was the sequel to a massive hit, a movie everyone knew would make a lot of money. That made their gesture even more generous.”

As a child, Quan also starred in Richard Donner’s 1985 film “The Goonies” as Data. He returned to the spotlight in 2023 after decades for “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” winning the Oscar for best supporting actor. His memoir, released Tuesday, details his early life fleeing Vietnam with his father, time in refugee camps, his life as a child actor and his triumphant return to the screen.

articles.title: ‘Resident Evil movies? I’ve never seen one’: Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchise
articles.summary: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger’s Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans.
body: Even if Cregger had not had a box-office smash that crossed over into awards contention, there would still be an atmosphere of hushed expectation around his next move. Both Barbarian and Weapons addressed hot-button issues – sexual assault and school shootings, respectively – while resisting easy interpretation. Both, too, started out seemingly heading in one narrative direction, before thrillingly careening off elsewhere. Thus, with just two features, Cregger had established a reputation for totally terrifying, utterly unpredictable and – most importantly – genuinely original movies.

Yet the real shocker from this nascent horror auteur is still to come. For his third film, Cregger has taken inspiration from existing intellectual property – or IP, those two little letters bound to strike fear into the heart of even the most stoic cineaste. Zach Cregger has made a Resident Evil movie.

articles.title: Ke Huy Quan on Receiving “Generous” $100K Residuals Check for ‘Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom’
articles.summary: The Oscar winner admitted he "didn’t understand how more money could suddenly appear" after already being compensated for his work on Steven Spielberg's 1984 film.
body: Ke Huy Quan is recalling his reaction to learning as a child that his first residual check for Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom was $100,000.

The Oscar winner opened up about the life-changing moment in his new memoir Never Say Die, which hit bookstands on Tuesday. Quan was only 12 years old when he booked his first major role as Short Round in Steven Spielberg ‘s 1984 film, so he didn’t realize he would receive residuals for the film in addition to his base pay for Temple of Doom.

The Everything Everywhere All at Once star continued, “They were both smiling, the kind of smile that comes from surprise and disbelief mixed together. They handed everything to me. It was a check from Lucasfilm. It was for almost $100,000, an amount that didn’t make any sense to me.”

Quan said he “didn’t understand how more money could suddenly appear” after already being compensated for his work on the follow-up to 1981’s Raiders of the Lost Ark. Once he wrapped his head around it, the Loki actor described the residuals clause as “a quiet gesture from Steven and George [Lucas].”

articles.title: Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist, Dies at 45
articles.summary: "He was a legendary musician, but his favorite accomplishment was being a husband and father. His biggest dreams came true," his band and wife wrote in a joint statement.
body: Chad Gilbert, the founding guitarist and backing vocalist of the punk rock band New Found Glory, died on Sunday. He was 45.

The band and Gilbert’s wife, Lisa Cimorelli, confirmed his death on Instagram, writing in a joint statement that he “passed away peacefully in his sleep” with “his wife and mother by his side, just as he wished.”
His cause of death wasn’t immediately available, but he previously opened up to People about his longtime battle with stage 4 adrenal cancer.

Born on March 9, 1981, in Coral Springs, Florida, Gilbert went on to form New Found Glory in 1997 with Jordan Pundik, Ian Grushka, Steve Klein and Joe Moreno, though the latter was quickly replaced by Cyrus Bolooki.

articles.title: The Twilight Zone's Rod Serling Wrote A Polarizing TV Adaptation Of A Beloved Book
articles.summary: The Twilight Zone creator Rod Serling adapted A Christmas Carol into a TV movie with heavy themes that didn't go over so well with some critics.
body: In the update, Ebenezer Scrooge is renamed Daniel Grudge, and he is infused with a very specific politic. At the beginning of the special, Grudge, a powerful industrialist, is lambasted by his nephew (a young Ben Gazzara) for canceling a foreign exchange program that the nephew had hoped to take part in. Grudge gives a speech about how America should adopt a noninterventionist, nativist standpoint, and never interact with other nations. He also talks about building up a stockpile of nuclear weapons, and putting the rest of the world on their back foot. Grudge's nephew argues that, no, America has enough resources to help others, and that a worldwide community of peace is a better idea.

Maybe you can now understand why some critics referred to "Carol for Another Christmas" as preachy and mawkish. Rod Serling clearly had a point to make, and just made it outright, rather than couching it in metaphor or story. The review from the New York Times, which I'll quote below, ripped into Serling's screenplay with savage enthusiasm.
points: The Twilight Zone creator Rod Serling adapted A Christmas Carol into a TV movie with heavy themes that didn't go over so well with some critics.

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone Learned About Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship While Watching TV: “It Won’t Work”
articles.summary: Last year, Donald Trump named Stallone, along with Jon Voight and Mel Gibson, as Hollywood's "special ambassadors" who "will be my eyes and ears" in the industry.
body: However, during a recent interview with The Sunday Times, Stallone revealed that he learned about his presidential appointment while watching television.

Stallone admitted he had reservations about the position “because Hollywood, I guess it’s like feudal states. They have their little kingdoms. You don’t go in and tell six studios how to do things. And Mel Gibson and Jon Voight, we’re kind of do-our-own-thing people. No, it won’t work.”

He also explained this to Trump. “I said thank you and ciao, because it’s impossible,” Stallone added. “Hollywood works and it will evolve. It’s corporate and corporate people won’t want to hear me tell them about finance.”

While Stallone has publicly supported Trump, previously introducing the president-elect at a party at Mar-a-Lago following his 2024 re-election, he’s also endorsed politicians across the political spectrum throughout his career. The Tulsa King actor has maintained, “I am not a political animal,” and “I’m almost a political atheist.”

articles.title: Lee Majors' First Credited Movie Role Was In This Rarely Talked About 1968 Western
articles.summary: Lee Majors made his first credited movie appearance in this forgotten 1968 Western that also featured Charlton Heston and Donald Pleasence.
body: Before he was the Six Million Dollar Man or the Fall Guy, Lee Majors introduced himself to mass audiences as Heath Barkley on the classic Western TV series "The Big Valley." But while he came to prominence as the hard-headed Barkley scion, Majors had actually been working in film and TV for some time and had worked alongside some of the greats. In 1968, for instance, he made his official movie debut in the oft-overlooked Western "Will Penney," which starred Donald Pleasance, Bruce Dern, and the great Charlton Heston.

Majors actually made his film debut in the 1964 William Castle horror "Strait-Jacket." Unfortunately he went uncredited for his contribution to the film. But it was a heck of a debut for the young star-in-the-making. For one thing, he was able to work with a horror legend in Castle, who six years prior had issued life insurance policies to viewers of his film "Macabre" in order to cover the possibility of them dying of fright during the movie. What's more, Majors arrived on-screen in spectacular fashion when the great Joan Crawford hacked off his head.

articles.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
articles.summary: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over from long-running presenting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.
body: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show with a revamped presenting line-up.
An average of 5.3 million viewers tuned in on Saturday with a share of 49.2% of the overnight ratings, which was 7% up on last year, and it remained high on iPlayer's most popular chart on Sunday.
Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut, taking over from Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left last year.
Famous faces including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips stepped on to the ballroom floor for the first time.
